\begin{abstract}
We extend the resolution-refinement-plus-rodeo pipeline that we implemented
and assessed on the pairing Hamiltonian~\cite{EigenQPairing2026} to the
Hubbard model, the standard testbed for strongly correlated fermions, and to
the form of refinement for which the method was originally proposed: a
\emph{lattice} refinement in which every coarse site is resolved into a block
of fine sites and the prolongation maps each coarse orbital onto the bonding
combination of its block.  The Galerkin projection of the fine Hubbard
Hamiltonian onto the prolonged subspace is again a Hubbard model: in one
dimension with $(t,U)\to(t/2,U/2)$, so that the refinement hierarchy is
self-similar at fixed $U/t$, and in two dimensions with $(t,U)\to(t/2,U/4)$.
All stages --- the coarse eigenstate, the prolonged state, the adiabatically
refined state and the rodeo-filtered state --- are benchmarked against exact
diagonalization in the conserved $(N_\uparrow,N_\downarrow)$ sector, using
the dense, Lanczos and matrix-free solvers of our ED code, and the same
matched-observable methodology as in Ref.~\cite{EigenQPairing2026}.  For the
open chain refined from four to eight sites with two particles per spin, the
prolonged state has a ground-state weight $p_0=0.75$--$0.81$ for $U/t=0$--$8$
and the shift-controlled refinement path brings it to $p>0.9999$ by $T=16/t$
at every $U$, although the sector gap of the fine Hamiltonian falls from
$0.53t$ to $0.14t$: the path conserves total spin and lattice symmetry, so
the gap that controls the refinement is the distance to the next state in the
symmetry sector of the target, $0.88t$--$0.37t$ here, not the sector gap.
The same protection lets the refinement $8\to16$ sites succeed at
$T=16/t$ with a fine-sector gap of $0.05t$.  The lesson has a sharp
converse: for the $2\times2\to4\times4$ plaquette refinement at
$(N_\uparrow,N_\downarrow)=(2,2)$ the coarse ground state is a $d$-wave
singlet and has \emph{zero} overlap with the $s$-wave fine ground state;
refining the nearly degenerate $s$-wave coarse state instead gives
$p=0.99997$ at $T=16/t$.  A two-local alternative to the projector path,
adiabatic ``un-dimerization'' of the fine lattice, refines as fast but is
capped by the finite-penalty ceiling $1-p\simeq(t/\Lambda)^2$; two rodeo
cycles remove either residual.  Chains that start from the filled dimer, a
single computational basis state, reach $p>0.999$ in two refinement steps
without any variational input.  \todo{Circuit-level numbers (Trotterized
refinement, controlled evolution, CNOT budgets), the UCCSD comparator and
the strong-coupling ($t$--$J$) limit are to be added.}
\end{abstract}

\maketitle

% ===========================================================================
\section{Introduction}
% ===========================================================================
In Ref.~\cite{EigenQPairing2026} we implemented, end to end and at the gate
level, a pipeline for eigenstate preparation in which an eigenstate of a
coarse Hamiltonian is lifted by a prolongation operator into a finer model
space, transported adiabatically along a shift-controlled, gapped path
(\emph{resolution refinement}~\cite{Bogner2026}) and then cleaned by the
rodeo algorithm~\cite{Choi2021,Qian2024}, a projective spectral filter.  The
testbed there was the constant-pairing Hamiltonian, exactly solvable by the
Richardson ansatz, with ``resolution'' meaning the number of single-particle
levels at fixed particle number, and the assessment was sober: at eight
qubits the refinement stage did not beat a cheap unitary coupled-cluster
input on gate count, and its merits were the absence of a classical
optimization loop and of training measurements.  A seniority-breaking
particle-hole interaction, added in Sec.~VI of that work, left the structure
and convergence of the pipeline unchanged while raising the depth of a
Trotter step ninefold.

The present paper carries the same pipeline, the same benchmarks and the
same cost accounting to the Hubbard model~\cite{Hubbard1963,Arovas2022},
\begin{equation}
  H=-\sum_{\langle ij\rangle\sigma}t_{ij}\big(c^\dagger_{i\sigma}c_{j\sigma}+\mathrm{h.c.}\big)
   +U\sum_i n_{i\uparrow}n_{i\downarrow},
  \label{eq:hubbard}
\end{equation}
for three reasons.  First, the Hubbard model is the canonical strongly
correlated fermion problem and the most frequently used benchmark for
quantum simulation of
fermions~\cite{Wecker2015,Cade2020,Cai2020,Stanisic2022}; it contains the
one-body particle-hole channel (hopping) that the pairing model lacks and
the two-body on-site term in their simplest forms, so it tests the lesson of
Sec.~VI of Ref.~\cite{EigenQPairing2026} on a model where the seniority
symmetry is absent from the outset.  Second, it is the setting for which
resolution refinement was proposed~\cite{Bogner2026}: a \emph{lattice}
refinement in which every coarse site is resolved into a block of fine
sites, the prolongation is a product of Givens rotations rather than the
gate-free embedding of the basis refinement, and the fine lattice is the
natural discretization of a continuum problem.  Third, the model is not
exactly solvable in general, so the exact-diagonalization (ED) reference
that anchored every number in Ref.~\cite{EigenQPairing2026} must now be
produced numerically; we keep that discipline and benchmark every stage
against ED in the conserved $(N_\uparrow,N_\downarrow)$ sector with the
dense, Lanczos and matrix-free solvers of our ED code~\cite{HubbardNotebook},
which also covers the $t$--$J$ model and the chain, square and checkerboard
lattices used below.

Two structural results make the lattice refinement of the Hubbard model
particularly clean.  The Galerkin projection of the fine Hubbard Hamiltonian
onto the prolonged subspace is itself a Hubbard model, with $(t,U)\to(t/2,U/2)$
in one dimension --- so the hierarchy of resolutions is self-similar at
fixed $U/t$ --- and $(t,U)\to(t/2,U/4)$ in two dimensions
(Sec.~\ref{sec:galerkin}).  And the interpolation path conserves total spin
and the point-group symmetry of the lattice, so the gap that controls the
adiabatic transport is the distance to the next state \emph{in the symmetry
sector of the target}, which stays of order $t$ while the sector gap of the
fine Hamiltonian collapses with $U$ and with system size
(Sec.~\ref{sec:symmetry}); the converse is that a coarse ground state in the
wrong irreducible representation cannot be refined at all
(Sec.~\ref{sec:2d}).

The paper follows the structure of Ref.~\cite{EigenQPairing2026}.
Section~\ref{sec:model} fixes the model, the sector encoding and the ED
reference.  Section~\ref{sec:pipeline} defines the lattice prolongation, the
Galerkin coarse Hamiltonian, the two refinement paths and the rodeo filter.
Section~\ref{sec:results} reports the preliminary sector-exact results for
the open chain ($2\to4\to8\to16$ sites) and the square plaquette
($2\times2\to4\times4$).  Section~\ref{sec:circuits} \todo{will} give the
Pauli structure of the Hubbard chain in the Jordan--Wigner encoding, the
cost of the prolongation and of the embedded coarse term, and the gate
budgets.  Section~\ref{sec:discussion} discusses the results, the
strong-coupling limit and the outlook.

% ===========================================================================
\section{The Hubbard model and its exact-diagonalization reference}
\label{sec:model}
% ===========================================================================
We use $t_{ij}=t=1$ on nearest-neighbor bonds, open boundary conditions
unless stated otherwise, and the lattices of Ref.~\cite{HubbardNotebook}:
the chain of $L$ sites, the $L\times L$ square lattice with site index
$i=xL+y$, and the checkerboard lattice, which adds both diagonals with
amplitude $\alpha t$ on the plaquettes whose lower-left corner has $x+y$
even.  The Hamiltonian conserves $N_\uparrow$ and $N_\downarrow$ separately,
and all calculations are done in one such sector of dimension
$\binom{N}{N_\uparrow}\binom{N}{N_\downarrow}$.

\paragraph{Encoding and ED.}
Spin-orbitals are Jordan--Wigner ordered in two blocks, the $N$ up orbitals
followed by the $N$ down orbitals.  With this ordering a down hop picks up
the parity of all up electrons twice, which cancels, so the sector
Hamiltonian factorizes exactly as
\begin{equation}
  H=K_\uparrow\otimes\mathbb 1+\mathbb 1\otimes K_\downarrow
   +U\,\mathrm{diag}(\text{double occupancy}),
  \label{eq:kron}
\end{equation}
where $K_\sigma$ is the one-species hopping matrix on the sorted occupation
masks of that species.  Reference energies and eigenvectors are obtained
with dense diagonalization up to a few thousand states and with ARPACK
Lanczos beyond; for the largest sectors the Hamiltonian is never stored,
the matrix-vector product being applied as
$K_\uparrow\Psi+\Psi K_\downarrow^{\mathsf T}+U(\mathrm{docc}\circ\Psi)$ on the
state reshaped as an up$\times$down matrix.  The code is validated against
free fermions at $U=0$, the analytic dimer
$E_0=\tfrac12(U-\sqrt{U^2+16t^2})$, the Heisenberg limit of the $t$--$J$
model at half filling and the hopping-induced resonating-valence-bond states
of the checkerboard lattice~\cite{HubbardNotebook}.  Every number quoted in
Sec.~\ref{sec:results} is compared with this reference, and the sector
dimensions encountered there range from $1$ (the filled dimer) to $14\,400$
(four particles on sixteen sites).

\paragraph{Why the Hubbard model after the pairing model.}
In the pairing model the seniority symmetry confines the ground state to a
subspace in which the UCCSD solver is a doubles theory and the refinement
path has large gaps; the particle-hole term of
Ref.~\cite{EigenQPairing2026} broke that symmetry by hand.  In
Eq.~\eqref{eq:hubbard} the hopping term is a one-body particle-hole operator
from the outset, single excitations do not vanish, and the only symmetries
left to the pipeline are the ones it inherits from the lattice: particle
number per spin, total spin $S$, and the point group.  These are exactly the
symmetries that, as we show, decide which gap governs the refinement.

% ===========================================================================
\section{The pipeline for lattice refinement}
\label{sec:pipeline}
% ===========================================================================

\subsection{Prolongation: coarse sites to blocks of fine sites}
\label{sec:prolong}
A refinement step maps a coarse lattice of $N_c$ sites onto a fine lattice of
$N_f=bN_c$ sites by resolving every coarse site $c$ into a block $B(c)$ of
$b$ fine sites, $b=2$ for the chain (sites $2c,2c+1$) and $b=4$ for the
square lattice ($2\times2$ plaquettes).  The prolongation sends the coarse
orbital to the normalized symmetric (bonding) combination of its block,
\begin{equation}
  c^\dagger_{c\sigma}\;\longmapsto\;
  s^\dagger_{c\sigma}=\frac{1}{\sqrt b}\sum_{f\in B(c)}c^\dagger_{f\sigma},
  \label{eq:bonding}
\end{equation}
and a coarse Slater determinant to the corresponding product of
$s^\dagger$ operators; particle numbers are unchanged, so the filling halves
(quarters) at each step, as it must for a sequence of lattices approaching
the continuum at fixed particle number~\cite{Bogner2026}.  The map
$P$ is an isometry, $P^\dagger P=\mathbb 1$, from the coarse sector of
dimension $\binom{N_c}{N_\uparrow}\binom{N_c}{N_\downarrow}$ into the fine
sector; its complement is spanned by configurations in which at least one
antibonding block mode $a^\dagger_{c\sigma}$ (and, for $b=4$, the two further
orthogonal block modes) is occupied.  On a quantum register in which the
fine qubits of a block are adjacent, $P$ is implemented by preparing the
coarse state on one qubit per block per spin and applying one Givens
rotation per block per spin (two for $b=4$) --- the ``two single-qubit
rotations and two CNOTs per site per spatial direction'' of
Ref.~\cite{EigenQPairing2026}, i.e.\ $O(N_c)$ two-qubit gates, in contrast
to the gate-free embedding of the basis refinement.  In the sector-basis
prototype used below, $P$ is built explicitly: for each coarse occupation
pattern the fine amplitudes are $b^{-n_\sigma/2}$ on every choice of one
fine site per occupied block, with the sign of the permutation that sorts
the chosen fine indices.

\subsection{The Galerkin coarse Hamiltonian}
\label{sec:galerkin}
The coarse Hamiltonian whose eigenstate is to be refined is the fine
Hamiltonian seen at coarse resolution, $\Hlow=P^\dagger\Hhigh P$.  This
choice makes the prolonged state satisfy $\expval{\Hhigh}{P\psi_{\rm low}}
=E_{\rm low}$ exactly, as in Ref.~\cite{EigenQPairing2026}, and it has a
closed form.  Projecting the fine hopping term with Eq.~\eqref{eq:bonding}:
an intra-block bond contributes $-t(n_s-n_a)$, i.e.\ a constant $-t$ per
particle on the prolonged subspace, and each inter-block bond contributes
$\tfrac12 s^\dagger_c s_{c'}$; projecting the on-site term,
$n_{f\sigma}\to n_{s_c\sigma}/b$ for every $f\in B(c)$, gives
$U\sum_{f\in B(c)}n_{f\uparrow}n_{f\downarrow}\to(U/b)\,n_{s_c\uparrow}n_{s_c\downarrow}$.
Hence
\begin{align}
  \text{chain:}\quad &\Hlow=H_{\rm Hubbard}\!\big(L;\,t/2,\,U/2\big)-tN, \label{eq:gal1d}\\
  \text{square:}\quad&\Hlow=H_{\rm Hubbard}\!\big(L\times L;\,t/2,\,U/4\big)-2tN, \label{eq:gal2d}
\end{align}
with $N=N_\uparrow+N_\downarrow$, and with the same boundary conditions as the
fine lattice.  Both identities were verified to machine precision against
the numerically projected matrices.  In one dimension the ratio $U/t$ is
preserved, so a chain of refinements $L\to2L\to4L\to\cdots$ is a sequence
of Hubbard chains with the same interaction strength and a hopping scale
that doubles at each step: the hierarchy is self-similar, and the coarsest
member can be the two-site dimer or, for $N=2L$, the filled dimer, a single
computational basis state.  In two dimensions the effective interaction of
the coarse model is weaker by a factor of two relative to its hopping.  We
note that the Galerkin pair $(\Hlow,\Hhigh)$ is a choice; a continuum-scaling
pair ($t\propto a^{-2}$, $U\propto a^{-1}$ in one dimension) would start the
path from a different coarse ground state and change only the initial
overlap $p_0$, not the construction.

\subsection{Two refinement paths}
\label{sec:paths}
\paragraph{Path A: the shift-controlled projector path.}
As in Ref.~\cite{EigenQPairing2026},
\begin{equation}
  H_A(s)=\cos^2\!\big(\tfrac{\pi s}{2}\big)P(\Hlow-\mu)P^\dagger
        +\sin^2\!\big(\tfrac{\pi s}{2}\big)(\Hhigh-\mu),\quad s=t/T,
  \label{eq:pathA}
\end{equation}
with the shift $\mu=E_{\rm low}+\mu_{\rm buf}$ placing the complement of the
prolonged subspace (where $P(\Hlow-\mu)P^\dagger$ vanishes) at energy
$\mu_{\rm buf}$ above the tracked state at $s=0$.  Because
$P(\Hlow-\mu)P^\dagger=\Pi_a(\Hhigh-\mu)\Pi_a$ with $\Pi_a$ the projector onto
empty antibonding modes, the coarse term is, on a device, the fine
Hamiltonian in the rotated (bonding/antibonding) frame conditioned on all
antibonding qubits being in $\ket{0}$ --- the multi-controlled structure whose
cost dominated the $3\to4$ chain of Ref.~\cite{EigenQPairing2026}, now with
$N_f/2$ control qubits per spin.

\paragraph{Path B: adiabatic un-dimerization.}
The same end points are connected by a path that stays two-local in the
laboratory frame: add to the fine Hamiltonian an extra hopping $\Lambda$ on
the intra-block bonds and switch it off,
\begin{equation}
  H_B(s)=\Hhigh-\Lambda\cos^2\!\big(\tfrac{\pi s}{2}\big)
  \sum_{\langle ff'\rangle\in\mathrm{intra}}\sum_\sigma
  \big(c^\dagger_{f\sigma}c_{f'\sigma}+\mathrm{h.c.}\big).
  \label{eq:pathB}
\end{equation}
At $s=0$ the antibonding modes are pushed up by $2\Lambda$, and for
$\Lambda\to\infty$ the ground state of $H_B(0)$ is the prolonged Galerkin
ground state; at finite $\Lambda$ it differs from it by an admixture of
order $t/\Lambda$, so a transport that starts from the prolonged state
carries a residual $1-p\simeq c\,(t/\Lambda)^2$ to the end.  Path~B is the
dimerized Hubbard chain (the plaquette Hubbard model in two dimensions)
being adiabatically made uniform; every Trotter step along it costs what a
step of the fine Hamiltonian costs, with no conditioning.  We compare the
two paths at equal $T$ and, in Sec.~\ref{sec:circuits}, at equal gate
count.

\paragraph{Refinement time.}
The exact evolution along either path is computed as in
Ref.~\cite{EigenQPairing2026}: the $s$ interval is split into $M_s$ slices
(96 here), the Hamiltonian at the slice midpoint is diagonalized once, and
the slice propagators are reused for every $T$.  We report the overlap
$p(T)=|\langle\Psi_{\rm high}|\psi(T)\rangle|^2$ with the exact fine ground
state on a grid of $T$ and quote $T^*$ as the first grid value with
$1-p(T)<10^{-3}$.  For the $14\,400$-dimensional sectors the slice
propagators are applied with a sparse Krylov exponential (48 slices).

\subsection{The rodeo filter}
\label{sec:rodeo}
The filter is unchanged from Ref.~\cite{EigenQPairing2026}: $M$ cycles of
the controlled evolution $e^{-i\Hhigh t_k}$ on one reused ancilla with the
phase $e^{i\Eobj t_k}$, Gaussian cycle times of RMS width $\sigma$, and
post-selection on the ancilla.  For an input
$\ket\psi=\sum_kc_k\ket{E_k}$ and $\Eobj=E_0$ the fidelity of the ensemble
of accepted runs obeys exactly
\begin{equation}
  1-\mathcal F_M=\frac{\sum_{k\neq0}|c_k|^2q_k^M}{p+\sum_{k\neq0}|c_k|^2q_k^M},
  \qquad q_k=\tfrac12\big(1+e^{-(E_k-E_0)^2\sigma^2/2}\big),
  \label{eq:fid}
\end{equation}
which we evaluate from the ED spectrum.  The width is set by the smallest
excitation energy that carries weight in the input,
$\sigma=5/\Deff$ (Sec.~\ref{sec:symmetry}); choosing it from the bare sector
gap would lengthen the controlled evolutions by a factor of up to three for
no gain.

Table~\ref{tab:chain48} summarizes the refinement of the four-site chain

$p_0=0.75$--$0.81$, with a weak maximum at $U=2t$; unlike the pairing

fine Hamiltonian falls by a factor of four over the range of $U$, from

scaling; the ceiling, not the transport, limits Path~B, and a schedule with
$\Lambda\to\infty$ at $s=0$ or a final filter removes it.

\subsection{Which gap controls the refinement: symmetry protection}
\label{sec:symmetry}
Both terms of Eq.~\eqref{eq:pathA} commute with the total spin and with
the point group of the fine lattice (the block structure respects the
reflection of the chain and the $C_{4v}$ group of the square), and the
prolongation maps irreducible representations onto themselves.  The
transported state therefore never leaves the symmetry sector of the coarse
ground state --- a spin singlet, even under reflection, for the cases of
Table~\ref{tab:chain48} --- and the states that can be excited along the
path are only those of the same sector.  The spectral decomposition of the
prolonged state makes this explicit: for $U=4t$ the lowest fine excitations
at $0.223t$ and $0.459t$ above the ground state carry weights below
$10^{-29}$, and the first state with nonzero weight ($4.6\times10^{-5}$)
lies at $\Deff=0.588t$; at $U=8t$ the corresponding numbers are $0.137t$,
$0.286t$ (zero weight) and $\Deff=0.366t$ (weight $3\times10^{-7}$), with
the bulk of the excited weight lying still higher.  $\Deff$ falls with $U$
much more slowly than $\Delta$, which explains the $U$-independent $T^*$ of
Table~\ref{tab:chain48} and the fact that the minimum of the global path
gap, which sits at $s=1$ for $\mu_{\rm buf}=2t$ in every case, is not the
relevant quantity.

The protection survives a doubling of the system: refining the eight-site
chain to sixteen sites at $(2,2)$ ($784\to14\,400$ states, $U=4t$) starts
from $p_0=0.869$, faces a fine-sector gap of only $0.051t$, and still
reaches $p=0.9993$ at $T=16/t$ and $0.99995$ at $T=32/t$, with
$E_{\rm low}=-6.8172$ and $E_{\rm high}=-7.2098$.  \todo{Compute $\Deff$
and the full $p(T)$ curve for $8\to16$; add the Jansen--Ruskai--Seiler
bound of Sec.~IV.E of Ref.~\cite{EigenQPairing2026} evaluated with
$\Deff$ rather than $\Delta$.}

\subsection{Bootstrapping from the filled dimer}
\label{sec:dimer}
The self-similarity of the one-dimensional hierarchy allows the chain of
refinements to start from the two-site dimer with $N_\uparrow=N_\downarrow=2$,
whose sector contains a single state --- both sites doubly occupied ---
with coarse energy $E_{\rm low}=2\cdot(U/2)-2t\cdot2=U-4t$.  This is the
analogue of the $k=2$ determinant that seeded the $k=2\to4$ chain in
Ref.~\cite{EigenQPairing2026}, and it requires no classical or variational
preprocessing.  Table~\ref{tab:dimer} shows the step $2\to4$: the
doubly-occupied seed is, as expected, a worse start as $U$ grows,
$p_0=0.80$ at $U=0$ down to $0.48$ at $U=8t$, but the effective gap is
large ($\Deff=2.2t$--$0.8t$) and $p>0.9997$ is reached by $T=16/t$ at every
$U$.  Composed with the $4\to8$ step of Table~\ref{tab:chain48}, the
eight-site ground state is reached from a single computational basis
state in two refinement steps of $T=16/t$ each, with $p>0.9999$ before any
filtering.  \todo{Run the composed chain $2\to4\to8\to16$ with the refined
(not exact) state as input of each step, as in the $3\to4$ chain of
Ref.~\cite{EigenQPairing2026}; compare with the single-shot $2\to8$ and
$2\to16$ refinements.}

\subsection{Two dimensions: the plaquette and the wrong symmetry sector}
\label{sec:2d}
For the square lattice the first step is $2\times2\to4\times4$.  With one
particle per spin ($16\to256$ states) the refinement behaves as in one
dimension: $p_0=0.80$--$0.85$ for $U/t=0,4,8$, $\Deff\simeq2.1t$--$2.2t$,
and $p>0.9998$ at $T=8/t$ (Table~\ref{tab:2d}).  With two particles per
spin ($36\to14\,400$ states, $U=4t$) the prolonged coarse ground state has
\emph{zero} overlap with the fine ground state.  The reason is the point
group: the half-filled plaquette ground state (Galerkin parameters
$t/2$, $U/4$) is the $d$-wave singlet that transforms as $B_1$ under
$C_{4v}$, whereas the ground state of four particles on the dilute
$4\times4$ lattice is the $s$-wave ($A_1$) singlet, and the prolongation,
which commutes with $C_{4v}$, cannot connect them.  The decomposition of
the fine ground state over the prolonged coarse eigenstates confirms it:
the coarse ground state carries weight $0$, the first excited coarse state,
only $0.071t$ above it and in $A_1$, carries $0.647$, all other coarse
states together $0.007$.  Refining that $A_1$ state along Path~A
($\mu=E_1^{\rm low}+2t$) reaches $p=0.99997$ at $T=16/t$ and $0.99999$ at
$T=32/t$, although the fine-sector gap is only $0.090t$: once the right
sector is chosen, the symmetry protection of Sec.~\ref{sec:symmetry} works
in its favor.

Two conclusions follow for the method.  The coarse state to be refined is
the lowest coarse eigenstate \emph{in the symmetry sector of the target},
which need not be the coarse ground state, and the coarse solver (UCCSD or
otherwise) must therefore be run with the target's quantum numbers imposed
or at least diagnosed; and the rodeo filter cannot rescue a wrong choice,
since a state of zero overlap has nothing to amplify.  Conversely, when the
coarse ground state is in the wrong sector the refinement becomes a
sensitive detector of a level crossing between the coarse and the fine
problem --- here between the $d$- and $s$-wave singlets as the filling goes
from one half to one eighth.  \todo{Classify the irreps explicitly (build
$S^2$ and the $C_{4v}$ characters in the sector basis); scan $U$ to locate
the coarse $B_1$--$A_1$ crossing; compute $\Deff$ in the $A_1$ sector.}

\subsection{Rodeo filtering of the refined state}
\label{sec:res-rodeo}
With $\sigma=5/\Deff$ ($5.7/t$ to $13.6/t$ for $U/t=0$ to $8$) the filter
applied to the prolonged state behaves as the pairing case did: the
infidelity falls from $1-p_0\simeq0.2$ to $4$--$5\times10^{-3}$ after six
cycles and $2$--$3\times10^{-4}$ after ten, the geometric $2^{-M}$
suppression of Eq.~\eqref{eq:fid}.  Applied to the Path-A state refined for
$T=16/t$ the same filter starts from $1-p\simeq10^{-4}$ and reaches
$0.5$--$1.4\times10^{-6}$ after six cycles; applied to the Path-B state
($\Lambda=16t$, $T=32/t$) it starts from the ceiling, $1-p\simeq2\times10^{-3}$,
and reaches $2$--$4\times10^{-5}$ after six cycles.  As in
Ref.~\cite{EigenQPairing2026}, the question that matters is not whether the
refined input converges faster per cycle --- it does, by the ratio of the
initial infidelities --- but whether the cycles saved pay for the
refinement gates; that comparison requires the circuit-level
Trotterization and is deferred to Sec.~\ref{sec:circuits}.  \todo{Add the
$M$-scans as a figure (prolonged, refined A at $T^*$ and $2T^*$, refined B,
UCCSD) and the acceptance probabilities.}

\section{Quantum circuits and depth comparison}
\label{sec:circuits}
% ===========================================================================
\todo{To be computed with the gate-level simulator of
Ref.~\cite{EigenQPairing2026} (16 qubits for the $L=8$ chain).  What can be
stated now:}
\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{Pauli structure of the fine chain.}  In the block
  Jordan--Wigner ordering of Sec.~\ref{sec:model} an open chain of $L_f$
  sites on $2L_f$ qubits has $4(L_f-1)$ hopping strings
  $\tfrac t2(X_jX_{j+1}+Y_jY_{j+1})$ of weight two, $L_f$ interaction strings
  $\tfrac U4Z_jZ_{j+L_f}$ and $2L_f$ single-$Z$ terms: 52 strings of weight
  $\le2$ for $L_f=8$, against the 325 strings of weight up to eight of the
  $k=4$ pairing model on half the qubits.  A second-order Trotter step costs
  of order $2\times(28+8)\times2=144$ CNOTs on all-to-all connectivity; the
  $Z_jZ_{j+L_f}$ terms are the only non-local ones and the site-major
  ordering, which makes them adjacent at the price of weight-three hopping
  strings, is the alternative to be compared.
  \item \textbf{Prolongation.}  $N_c$ Givens rotations per spin between
  adjacent qubits ($2$ CNOTs each): 16 CNOTs for $4\to8$.
  \item \textbf{Coarse term of Path~A.}  In the rotated frame the fine
  Hamiltonian acquires inter-block terms coupling bonding and antibonding
  modes and on-site terms of weight four, and the coarse term is the
  bonding-mode Hubbard chain conditioned on the $L_f$ antibonding qubits;
  its cost is to be counted as in Sec.~V.A of
  Ref.~\cite{EigenQPairing2026} and is the main motivation for Path~B,
  whose steps cost exactly a fine-Hamiltonian step plus the intra-block
  hopping already present.
  \item \textbf{Budgets.}  CNOTs per accepted preparation for the prolonged,
  Path-A, Path-B and UCCSD inputs at matched infidelity, Trotter floor,
  controlled evolution of the rodeo cycles, and the sufficient conditions
  versus practice, all as in Secs.~V.B--V.C and IV.E of
  Ref.~\cite{EigenQPairing2026}.
\end{itemize}

% ===========================================================================
\section{Discussion and outlook}
\label{sec:discussion}
% ===========================================================================
\todo{Points to make, in the order of the paper-1 discussion:}
\begin{itemize}
  \item The lattice refinement of the Hubbard model is structurally cleaner
  than the basis refinement of the pairing model: a Galerkin coarse model in
  closed form, a self-similar hierarchy in one dimension, a two-local
  Hamiltonian, a prolongation of $O(N_c)$ gates.  Against this stands a
  coarse term that is conditioned on $L_f$ qubits, and Path~B as its
  two-local replacement with a $(t/\Lambda)^2$ ceiling.
  \item Which gap matters: the symmetry-protected effective gap $\Deff$,
  not the sector gap; this is why $T^*$ is flat in $U$ and in size here,
  and it suggests that the inverse-gap scaling extracted in
  Ref.~\cite{EigenQPairing2026} through the shift should be re-read as a
  statement about $\Deff$.  Its converse, the zero-overlap plaquette, is a
  warning for any refinement or nucleation scheme: the coarse state must
  carry the quantum numbers of the target.
  \item Strong coupling.  At fixed $U/t$ the hierarchy is self-similar, so
  refinement does not by itself reach the $t$--$J$ regime; a path that
  raises $U$ along with the resolution, or a refinement at fixed filling
  (prolonging with doubled particle number, which is not a state map) are
  the options, and the ED code's $t$--$J$ solver gives the reference.  The
  rodeo filter, in contrast, applies unchanged to the $t$--$J$ Hamiltonian
  in its constrained sector.  \todo{Decide whether a $t$--$J$ section
  belongs in this paper.}
  \item Relation to nucleation~\cite{Sadia2026}: in one dimension the
  dimer-seeded hierarchy and the nucleation of a chain from a dimer start
  from the same state and reach the same target by refining resolution
  versus growing the domain; the Hubbard chain is the natural place to
  compare the two paths at matched gate count.
  \item Hardware targets: the $4\to8$ chain (16 qubits) and the
  $2\times2\to4\times4$ plaquette at $(1,1)$ (32 qubits, 256-dimensional
  sector) are within reach of current devices; the Trotter step is shallow.
\end{itemize}
